opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I like it mostly because it's the definition that cuts through the most nonsense. When people argue about intelligence, they very quickly get pulled into these philosophical tar pits: is it consciousness, is it understanding, does it really "know" things, is there something it's like to be the system? Those are interesting questions, I'm not dismissing them, but they're not the questions that matter when you're trying to figure out whether something is going to change the world, or whether it's dangerous.

What matters, practically, is: can the thing get stuff done? Can you give it a goal, or can it have a goal, and can it find a way to achieve that goal in a complex, messy environment? That's what humans have that chimpanzees don't. It's not that we're more conscious or have nicer feelings. It's that we can build rockets and nuclear weapons and agriculture. We can solve problems across an absurdly wide range of domains. That's the thing that made us the dominant species on this planet, for better or worse.

So when I think about AI, the question I care about isn't "is GPT really thinking?" It's "what can it do?" If a system can solve problems as well as or better than humans across a wide range of domains, then from the perspective of what happens to the world, it doesn't really matter whether it has some ineffable inner spark. The consequences are the same. A system that can outmaneuver you doesn't need to "truly understand" anything to outmaneuver you.

It's also nice because it's operational. You can measure it, at least in principle. You can look at a system and ask: what's the space of problems it can solve, how efficiently, how robustly, how general is it? That gives you something to work with, rather than endless debates about definitions that never terminate.

And there's a deeper point. Problem solving is fundamentally about optimization, about steering the world toward certain states and away from others. Once you frame intelligence that way, it becomes very clear why it's powerful and why it's potentially dangerous. A really good optimizer pointed at the wrong target is a really big problem. That framing makes the alignment problem obvious in a way that fuzzier definitions tend to obscure.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the range and space of problems a system can solve, but does not explain that which problems count as relevant can be selected according to the inquiry.

fable-5.1.text:
I like it because it's the least mystical definition I can find that still does all the work I need it to do. People love to argue about what intelligence "really is." Is it consciousness, is it creativity, is it understanding, is it some ineffable spark? And I think most of those debates are basically confused. They smuggle in a lot of human-centric baggage and then act surprised when the definition doesn't generalize.

If instead you say intelligence is the ability to solve problems, to take some goal state and actually get there across a wide range of environments, then you've got something operational. You can ask: how big is the set of problems this thing can solve? How efficiently does it solve them? How well does it transfer to problems it hasn't seen before? Those are real questions with real answers. You can measure them, or at least approximate them. You're not stuck arguing about whether a system "truly" understands anything.

It also cuts through a lot of the goalpost-moving we see in AI. Every time a system does something, people say "well, that's not real intelligence, it's just pattern matching" or "it's just statistics." Fine. But it solved the problem. If it can solve more and more problems, in more and more domains, with less and less hand-holding, then whatever you want to call the inside of the box, the outside of the box is getting more capable. And from a safety perspective, the outside of the box is what matters. A system that can solve the problem of acquiring resources, or persuading humans, or writing code that modifies its own training, is dangerous regardless of whether it has an inner life.

There's a nice connection to the more formal framings too, something like Legg and Hutter's definition of universal intelligence, or the work on optimization power, where you think about how well an agent achieves goals weighted over possible environments. The problem-solving framing is basically the plain-English version of that. It makes intelligence a property of a system's relationship to a space of tasks, not a property of its substrate. Which is exactly how I think we should be treating it.

The one caveat I'd add is that "problem" is doing a lot of lifting. You need to be clear about which problems, in which environments, and under what constraints. A chess engine is extremely intelligent on the problem "win at chess" and completely useless on everything else. So what people usually mean by general intelligence is breadth: the ability to solve problems you weren't specifically built for. And that's really the thing we're worried about with AGI. Not that it's smart in a narrow slice, but that the set of problems it can solve starts to include problems like "how do I get the humans to stop interfering with me."

r001.rationale: The candidate says the problem set and environments must be specified, and describes measuring intelligence by the problems relevant to the task or inquiry.

astra-6.text:
I like it because it’s a pragmatic definition. It takes something that people tend to treat as mysterious and asks: what can this system actually do? Can it solve the problem in front of it? Can it figure out a solution when you haven’t explicitly told it how?

And it doesn’t presuppose that intelligence has to look human. A system might solve problems in a completely alien way, and I still want to be able to call that intelligent. I don’t want the definition to depend on whether it talks like us or whether we think it has an inner experience.

Of course, it’s not a complete measurement scheme. You still have to ask which problems, under what conditions, with how much time and computation. But I think that’s useful, because those are concrete questions. It moves the discussion from arguing about the essence of intelligence to talking about capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says to ask “which problems,” so it leaves the problem set unspecified, but it does not explain that the relevant set can be selected according to the inquiry.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it makes the concept concrete. If you say something is intelligent, I want to ask, “Okay, what can it actually do? What problems can it solve?” That gives us something to talk about beyond whether it looks human or produces an impressive explanation.

And “problem” is a very broad category here. Predicting the next word is a problem. Figuring out how to build a bridge is a problem. Navigating a social situation is a problem. You have some situation, some constraints, and some outcome you’re trying to achieve. Intelligence is the ability to figure out how to get there.

It’s certainly not a complete mathematical definition. You still have to specify which problems, under what conditions, with how much time and computation. But I like it as a starting point because it doesn’t require us to settle questions about consciousness or whether a system thinks the way we do before we can discuss its capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says problems form a broad category and that one must specify which problems are relevant, leaving the class open to be chosen for the discussion.
